Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)
- Assessment summary (transcript + DDx alignment):
  - Clinical presentation: sore throat followed by dry cough for ~1 week, transient fever early in course, now fluctuating symptoms with exertional shortness of breath, reported wheeze and chest discomfort. No hemoptysis, no weight loss, no persistent high fever. No objective exam findings recorded.
  - DDx concordant: acute viral upper respiratory infection with viral bronchitic reaction is the most likely diagnosis; viral-induced reactive airways disease/new-onset asthma is a possible contributor; atypical/early community-acquired pneumonia is less likely but possible.
- Diagnostic reasoning (from DDx, consistent with transcript):
  - Viral URI / viral bronchitis — High likelihood: timeline, symptom pattern (sore throat → dry cough), transient fever, fluctuating course.
  - Viral-induced reactive airways disease/new-onset asthma — Moderate likelihood: new wheeze and exertional dyspnea after viral prodrome; no prior asthma history and no objective lung exam or peak flow documented.
  - Atypical pneumonia (eg, Mycoplasma) — Low–Moderate likelihood: chest pain and exertional breathlessness could reflect lower respiratory involvement but absence of systemic toxicity and lack of focal signs reduce probability.
- Contradictions/conflicts:
  - DOB recorded in transcript as 9 May 2016 (implying age ~9 years) but conversation content (employment, request for sick note, phrasing) is inconsistent with a child; DDx and transcript note this discrepancy. Conflict noted.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)
- 1) Acute viral upper respiratory infection (viral pharyngitis with viral bronchitis) — High likelihood.
  - Justification: Sore throat followed within 1–2 days by dry, non-productive cough; transient fever early in course; fluctuating symptoms over ~1 week; no red-flag systemic features documented.
- 2) Viral-induced reactive airways disease / new-onset asthma — Moderate likelihood.
  - Justification: New wheeze and exertional shortness of breath starting after viral prodrome; consistent temporal relation though no prior asthma history or objective measures (wheeze on auscultation/peak flow) documented.
- 3) Atypical/early community-acquired pneumonia (eg, Mycoplasma) — Low–Moderate likelihood.
  - Justification: Chest discomfort and exertional breathlessness could indicate lower respiratory involvement; overall mild course and absence of focal findings or persistent high fever make this less likely than viral causes.
